stimulus.text: The 1771 map by Thomas Hutchins marks the village of Cahokia on the Mississippi River, near present-day St. Louis. The pre-contact city of Cahokia stood in this same river valley centuries earlier. Archaeologists who have mapped Cahokia describe a city of mounds, plazas, and a wooden palisade. Trade goods from far away reached the city: copper from the Great Lakes and shells from the Gulf Coast.
stimulus.source_note: Map from the shared image pool; Thomas Hutchins (1771), public domain. Archaeological description paraphrased from standard accounts of Cahokia.

stem: This 1771 map marks Cahokia on the Mississippi River, near present-day St. Louis. Mississippian chiefdoms like Cahokia built their towns in the river valleys of the Southeast and Midwest. Which factor best explains this location pattern?

options.text: River valleys provided fertile floodplain soils for the maize surpluses chiefdoms depended on.
The Mexica Empire in central Mexico had already claimed all the uplands.
options.misconception: Puts the Mexica in the Mississippi Valley, far from central Mexico.

options.text: Spanish officials ordered Native towns to be built along rivers for easier control.
options.misconception: Credits Spanish officials with towns that predate Spanish rule in the region.

options.text: Rivers were the only source of drinking water anywhere in North America.
options.misconception: Confuses fertile farmland with drinking water, which existed in many places.

rationales.A: Mississippian chiefdoms were maize-farming societies, and river floodplains gave them the rich soils that made large maize harvests possible.
rationales.B: The Mexica Empire was centered in central Mexico, far from the Mississippi Valley, so it claimed no uplands there.
rationales.C: These towns and their locations predate Spanish colonization of the region, so Spanish officials ordered nothing of the kind.
rationales.D: Fresh water existed in many places; the key advantage of river valleys was fertile farmland, not drinking water.
rationales.general:
1. Read the map. Cahokia sits on the Mississippi River, near present-day St. Louis.
2. Start with background, not the map: Mississippian chiefdoms farmed maize in the river valleys.
3. Ask what rivers give farmers. Each flood lays down fresh rich soil, a free delivery of fertilizer that keeps harvests large.
4. Connect place and food. Rich river soil grew the surpluses that fed chiefdom towns.
Remember: to explain where people settled, ask what the land gave them to eat.
